messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan Chaudhary is a 75-year-old South Asian man who came to the United States as a refugee decades ago and has spent the better part of his adult life working as a potter in a small studio attached to his home in a mid-sized American city. He lives with his wife of fifty years. He was referred for psychological assessment after his primary care physician noted significant functional decline and persistent sleep disturbance, and after Rajan himself, at his wife's quiet insistence, finally admitted that something had been wrong for a very long time.

The events that brought Rajan to this country unfolded across several months of communal violence in the region where he was born. He was in his mid-twenties when the killing began. What he carries most viscerally from that period is not a single moment but a sustained atmosphere of terror — the sound of vehicles moving slowly through narrow streets at night, which always preceded raids; the sight of uniformed men moving through his neighbourhood with absolute authority, deciding who stayed and who did not; and, above all, the funerals. There were many funerals in those months, held quickly and without ceremony, bodies lowered into earth while families looked over their shoulders. Rajan helped carry at least three of those bodies. He does not speak of this directly. He has never been able to find the words for what those weeks were, and when he tries, the images come not as a narrative but as shards — a specific quality of light, the sound of a car engine idling, the colour of a uniform — arriving without context or sequence, feeling, he has said, more present and more real than anything that happened yesterday.

He arrived in the United States and built a life. The potter's wheel became the organizing principle of that life: the discipline of clay, the patience it required, the way a form could be coaxed into being over hours. For many years, work was also a kind of refuge. But over the past several years, and with increasing intensity in the last eighteen months, Rajan has found himself unable to sustain the concentration that throwing requires. He sits at the wheel and his hands, which once moved with practiced certainty, falter. He has come to believe that he is no longer the craftsman he was — that whatever defined him as a maker of things has been taken from him — and this belief sits in him like a stone. Several commissions have gone unfulfilled. A gallery relationship he had maintained for over two decades has quietly ended.

Outside the studio, his world has contracted around a set of arrangements that feel, to him, like simple common sense. He does not attend funerals. When a neighbour died last spring and his wife asked him to accompany her to the service, he told her he was unwell, and she did not press him. He avoids the cemetery that sits four blocks from their home, rerouting his walks without ever explaining why. When he hears a car idling outside — especially at night, especially a heavier engine — he moves to a window and stands there, scanning the street methodically, watching until the vehicle leaves. He does the same in public spaces: his eyes move continuously across exits, across faces, across anything that might signal what is coming. When a police officer is visible — at a crossroads, outside a store — Rajan will cross the street or wait, and he has told his wife only that he finds such encounters uncomfortable. He has declined several family celebrations in recent years, including a grandchild's birthday gathering, because he was certain that feeling happy or hopeful in such settings would be followed by something terrible. The logic feels unassailable to him. He has also stopped voicing any disagreement, even mild, in family conversations, having concluded that he cannot manage the aftermath of conflict — that even the smallest upset now exceeds what he is capable of bearing.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a moment at the wheel three weeks ago when he simply stopped, sat with his hands in wet clay, and wept without knowing why. He has told his therapist that he does not expect to feel better — he is not sure he believes that is possible — but that he would like, before he dies, to finish one more piece of work that he is proud of.
